part1-import-rules.desc: Verifies that a file's imports only point: - Sideways (to siblings in its own module); or - Deeper (into nested modules) And that they never point (violations): - Up to a parent module; or - Across into a different branch of the tree
part1-import-rules.exception: Imports to a common module (see below section). If a common module is at `crate::app::[common]`, any files at or below `crate::app` may import it.
part1-import-rules.rationale: To keep a predictable module tree structure, where we know everything in a module's submodules are supporting logic for the module to call, and not the other way around (i.e. where submodules call up to their parent modules for supporting logic).

more-details.detail: Sideways/deeper imports must be written with `super::...` (i.e. never `crate::...`).
Imports to a common module (which isn't a sibling) must be written with `crate::...` (i.e. never `super::super...`).
more-details.rationale: To make the code more readable by distinguishing between a sideways/deeper import and an import up and 1 over to a common module.

common-modules.desc: These are modules for shared code. The following are their names and what they are for: - c: free-functions - t: types - s: `static` items - cnst: `const` items - ext_traits: extension trait definition and implementations Each may be a folder (e.g. `t/`) with a mod.rs file, or a single-file module (e.g. `t.rs`)
common-modules.example: - `crate::c` is the whole-crate shared free-functions, reachable everywhere
common-modules.note: Inside a common folder, the imports must still be sideways or deeper (i.e. `c/foo/bar.rs` cannot import `c/util.rs`, which sits above it, just because they are both in `c/`). A common folder re-roots the tree: inside it, the same up/across prohibitions apply, but measured from the common folder rather than the crate.
common-modules.rationale: There must be a way to share certain items between separate modules that have different submodules, because otherwise it would be impossible to write DRY code. In fact, this might be exaggerating it, but it would maybe even be impossible to write code at all. So, if we didn't have these common modules, the import rules would be too strict to work.

part2-item-homes.desc: Verifies that the following top-level items are only defined as public in the following common modules: - `static`: `s` - `const`: `cnst` - `struct`, `enum`, and `type` alias: `t` - `trait`: `t` and `ext_traits`
part2-item-homes.rationale: We want consistent locations for all user defined items

part3-common-publics.desc: Verifies that files in the following common modules only contain the following top-level items as public: - `s`: `static` - `cnst`: `const` - `t`: `struct`, `enum`, `type` alias, and `trait` - `ext_traits`: `trait` - `c`: `fn`
part3-common-publics.exemption: Items restricted to a visibility that cannot escape the common module (i.e. `pub(super)`)
part3-common-publics.rationale: We want consistent items on the public surface of common modules

part4-common-nesting.desc: Verifies that no common modules are nested in other common modules.
part4-common-nesting.rationale: Make reasoning about common modules easier

exception.desc: `c` modules may be nested inside `c` modules (e.g. `/c/foo/c/bar`). There may be as much nesting of these as desired.
exception.rationale: It's commonly necessary to nest `c` modules to share code within a `c` module.

part5-common-reexports.desc: For `t`, `s`, `cnst`, and `ext_traits` common modules, verifies that every module declaration in all mod.rs files are: - Private (i.e. `mod x;`, never `pub mod x;`); and - Glob re-exported (i.e. `pub use x::*;`).
part5-common-reexports.rationale: So that users can import `use ...::t::TypeName` (i.e. not `use ...::t::submodule::TypeName`), saving characters.
part5-common-reexports.exception: The glob re-export is not required when the module exposes no public items to re-export (e.g. a module containing only `impl` blocks).

part6-c-publics.desc: Verifies that all `mod.rs` files in a `c` common module: - Declares all of its modules as public (i.e. `pub mod ...`); and - Contains no `use` statements.
part6-c-publics.rationale: So callers of the `c` module can import the submodules and call the functions (e.g. submodule::fn_name())
part6-c-publics.exception: If the module contains a nested `c` module, the `mod.rs` must instead: - Declare the nested module privately as `mod c;` (annotated with the outer attribute `#[allow(clippy::module_inception)]` if a `c` module is the direct parent); and - Have a single `pub use c::*;` glob statement re-exporting the nested `c` module.

part7-impl-locations.desc: Verifies that all impls: - Live in a `t` common module; and - Are in the same file or a sibling file of the type's definition.
part7-impl-locations.exceptions: - For foreign types (i.e. not defined in our crate; like: `impl SomeTrait for Vec<T>`), the impl must live in an `ext_traits` common module. - For private types, impls in the same file as the type definition are allowed.
part7-impl-locations.rationale: To have an expected location for impls. Also, part of the effort to encourage small impls, preferring free-functions over methods.

part8-c-fns-used.desc: Verify that all public functions in a `c` common module are called in 2 or more distinct child branches of the directory that the `c` module is in.
part8-c-fns-used.rationale: A function in a `c` module is there because it's needed in multiple child branches. If a function is only used in one branch, it can be moved to that branch.

shared-privates.desc: The branch test is applied per cluster of public functions, not per function. Two public functions in the same file are in the same cluster when they both transitively reach a private item of that file (a private fn, type, or its impls). A cluster's callers are pooled, so a public function used in only one branch still passes when a cluster-mate is used in a different one. When a whole cluster is confined to one branch, every member is reported.
shared-privates.rationale: The rationale above ("it can be moved to that branch") is false when the function is a thin wrapper over private helpers that another branch also depends on: moving it would either duplicate those helpers or force them public, which in turn forces their types into a `t` module. Without this, such code has nowhere natural to live.
shared-privates.note: Reachability is a name-based heuristic: an item references a private name if that identifier appears anywhere inside it. It can over-link (a local variable sharing a private item's name), which only ever loosens the check, never tightens it.
shared-privates.unaffected: The "is never called" violation stays per-function; a dead public function is not rescued by its cluster-mates.

config.item: ignore_export_macros - when true, imports of macros that use `#[macro_export]` are exempt (default false)
